meta.homeTitle: Leon · Cited answers from your company’s tools
meta.homeDescription: Leon indexes your team’s tools and AI conversations, answers questions with a citation for every sentence, and says so when nothing on record supports an answer.
meta.useCasesDescription: How leadership, sales, support, product, project and onboarding teams use Leon: the questions they ask and the cited answers they get.
meta.connectorsDescription: {count} connectors across engineering, meetings, project management, CRM, support, email and files, synced every 15 minutes, plus your AI assistant conversations.
meta.productDescription: How Leon works: incremental sync from your tools, verbatim storage, hybrid full-text and vector search, and answers that cite every claim.
meta.securityDescription: Tenant isolation with Postgres row-level security, permissions enforced before ranking, private AI conversations, AES-256-GCM encrypted credentials, and a public list of what is still missing.
meta.documentationDescription: Connect Leon to your coding tools, by asking Claude Code or with one command in a terminal. What you need, what is sent, and how to disconnect.
meta.pricingDescription: A free pilot with one team, then a proposed €25 per active user per month once billing is in place. No commitment.

home.title: Know exactly what you promised.
home.lead: Leon reads your team’s tools and answers in plain English. Every sentence links to the original. When nothing on record supports an answer, it says so.
home.assistantTitle: Give your AI assistant your team’s context.
home.assistantLead: Leon’s MCP server exposes seven tools to any MCP client: search, fetch a source, list your threads of work on a repository, read one, read its past states, get the morning briefing, save a note. Paste its address into your assistant and authorize it in Leon: the access is revocable and inherits your permissions exactly.

assistantPoints.briefing: Your coding assistant opens each session with the morning briefing.
assistantPoints.sessions: Coding sessions are captured when they end, text only.
assistantPoints.log: Each source your assistant opens in full is written to an audit log.

home.ctaText: Create a workspace, connect your first tool, and ask your first question.
home.rule1Title: Every highlighted word comes from its source.
home.rule1Lead: A pink word, a pink number, a pink original. Pick a number and read the source it comes from.
home.rule2Title: When the record is silent, Leon says so.
home.rule2Lead: No source, no claim. Ask about something nobody wrote down and the answer is “I don’t know”, with the closest thing on record.
home.rule3Title: Leon sees what you see. Nothing more.
home.rule3Lead: Every answer is built only from what the person asking can open. Your email, Slack, Drive and AI conversations stay yours.
home.connLead: Connect a tool in one click or with an API key. Leon picks up changes every 15 minutes and keeps each item word for word. Your team keeps working where it already works.
home.connExtension: A browser extension brings in your conversations with AI assistants, private to you.
home.briefLead: What you did, what changed, what is still open. 250 words at most, each line with its source.
home.briefSmall: Your own AI assistant can ask Leon too, with your permissions.
home.secTitle: What is in place, and what is in progress.

product.heroTitle: Everything your team writes and says, indexed and cited.
product.heroLead: Leon syncs your tools and AI assistants, stores every item verbatim, keeps AI conversations private to their author, and answers with sentence-level citations.
product.flowCaption: The four stages: capture, store, search, chat.

documentation.heroTitle: Connect Leon to your coding tools.
documentation.heroLead: Two ways to do it: ask Claude Code to install it, or paste one command in a terminal. Either way, you authorize the computer in your browser.

requirements.title: What you need
requirements.lead: Four things, on the computer you want to connect.
requirements.system: A Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), or a Linux on x64 or arm64 with glibc (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora…). Windows, Alpine and the other Linux systems with musl are not supported: the command stops before it writes anything.
requirements.claude: At least one coding tool installed on this computer: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Antigravity. leon setup connects each one it finds, after showing its own text of what will be sent.
requirements.account: A Leon account. You sign in in your browser when you authorize the computer.

claude.title: Ask Claude Code
claude.lead: The simplest way. The button copies instructions: paste them into Claude Code and it does the setup with you.
claude.askTitle: What Claude Code will ask you
claude.ask1: Its permission to run the install command.
claude.ask2: Probably also to run it outside its sandbox (the isolated zone where it runs its commands), which may forbid writing in ~/.leon, downloading from nodejs.org, opening your browser or listening on 127.0.0.1 (your own computer only), which signing in does.
claude.ask3: Your agreement before it finishes the setup with the --yes option. It must first copy to you, as is and without summarizing, what will be sent (see “What is sent”). Without your explicit agreement, it does not run it. --yes gives no usage by itself: you choose them with the boxes of the authorization page.
claude.ask4: A click on “Authorize” in your browser, and your choice in its boxes: the usages checked by default, such as reading Leon (see “What is sent”), that your coding tools do not have yet. Claude Code warns you before it runs the command, which waits for that click for 5 minutes at most (about 100 seconds when the computer is already connected and the command opens the page again for the boxes), and reminds you that it ran it for you. The instructions forbid it from ticking, unticking or clicking anything on that page, and from opening its address in a browser it controls.
claude.end: At the end, it tells you which coding tools are connected and which Leon account the computer is connected to. The instructions forbid it from asking for, reading or showing a token.
claude.unavailable: The address of this Leon is not one the install command accepts, so the button is not offered here. The commands below show the address to replace.

terminal.title: In a terminal
terminal.lead: Open a terminal on the computer you want to connect and paste this command.
terminal.leadGeneric: Open a terminal on the computer you want to connect and paste this command, with the address of your Leon in place of the one shown.
terminal.step1: downloads the official Node of the version Leon pinned and Leon’s command-line tool (a single file, served by Leon), checks their SHA-256 and puts them in ~/.leon;
terminal.step2: runs leon setup: it writes the launcher ~/.leon/bin/leon, connects the computer (see “Authorize the computer”), looks for your coding tools, shows you what will be sent, asks for your agreement, then sets up the Claude Code hooks (small programs that Claude Code runs at the start and at the end of each session).
terminal.scope: It writes only in ~/.leon, plus the settings of your coding tools after you agree: nothing in your PATH, nothing in your shell profile. The commands below are therefore written with the full path, ~/.leon/bin/leon.
terminal.again: You can run it again at any time: what is already in place is not rewritten, and the command-line tool is brought to the version Leon serves.

authorize.title: Authorize the computer
authorize.p1: Your browser opens on a Leon page. Sign in if needed: the page then asks “Authorize this computer to send your coding sessions to Leon, in the … workspace?”. Click “Authorize” only if you just ran the command, yourself or by asking Claude Code to; otherwise click “Cancel”. When leon setup opens it, the page can also show boxes, checked by default, for the usages your coding tools do not have yet (today, reading Leon: see “What is sent”). They are yours: untick what you don’t want, then click “Authorize”. An unticked box is kept as a refusal and is not asked again; “Cancel” decides nothing.
authorize.p2: If the browser does not open, the command prints the address to open. It waits 5 minutes at most (100 seconds when leon setup --yes opens the page again on a computer that is already connected); Ctrl+C cancels without writing anything.
authorize.p3: Once the computer is authorized, the command shows the workspace and the account it is connected to (“Connected to … as …”) and keeps the connection in ~/.leon/connexion.json, readable only by your account on the computer. The token is created on your computer: the browser only sees its fingerprint.
authorize.shared: On a computer where several accounts are open at the same time, the other accounts can read the authorization address (on Linux, in /proc), and one of them could authorize it with their own Leon account: your token would then be registered on theirs. So check the account the command shows; if it is not yours, run ~/.leon/bin/leon logout. Or use ~/.leon/bin/leon login --with-token, which relies on a token created in Settings instead of that address.

sent.title: What is sent
sent.lead: In short, the text leon setup shows you before it sets up the hooks (nothing is written in the Claude Code settings before you agree). That is the text you accept, in the terminal or, with Claude Code, by telling it to use --yes. --yes gives no usage by itself: each usage below is asked separately, in the terminal or, for reading Leon only, with a box of the authorization page when leon setup opens it.
sent.where: The hooks go in your personal Claude Code settings: they run in all your sessions, in all your folders, personal ones included. A session started by a script (claude -p) runs them too, except with --bare, which loads no hooks.
sent.end: At the end of each session, the Leon server receives the text of the exchanges (your messages and Claude’s answers; the messages Claude Code adds in your place, such as a background task’s result, the output of a ! or / command, another session’s message or a script’s prompt, labeled as not typed by you; a ! command you type is sent whole) and the actions of the session, read from its transcript: the files written (paths in the repository), the commands run (only their executable, plus the subcommand for a fixed list of developer tools such as git, gh, pnpm or docker; never their other arguments), Git (branch, commits, pull requests), the task list, and a few markers (start and end times, number of messages and tool errors, whether the session used the web, an MCP server, a subagent or a network command).
sent.tools: Codex, Cursor and Antigravity, when leon setup finds their settings folder (for Antigravity, one of its own folders under ~/.gemini: ~/.gemini alone, the folder of Gemini CLI, is not enough), each show their own text first. After each turn, the Leon server receives the new exchanges and the actions of the session, read from the tool’s own file; the messages the tool writes itself in your place (a subagent’s report, a notification; with Codex, a ! command with its output) are sent too, labeled as written by the tool, not by you; the context the tool adds itself is not sent. What a hook missed is sent in the background the next time Leon’s start hook runs on this computer: at the start of a Claude Code or Codex session, or at the first message of a Cursor or Antigravity conversation. The usages below (lecture, resume) are offered to them too, with the same texts.
sent.secrets: Secrets are masked before sending, and again by the server.
sent.start: At the start of each session, the server receives the project key, the current Git branch and the session id. It sends back your recent sessions on this repository (their branch, pull requests, commits, files and remaining tasks) and the project’s morning briefing: Claude Code adds this block to the session context, so it is given to Claude Code’s model. With the lecture usage (below), it sends back instead of your recent sessions the summary of your work threads on this repository and an instruction to read the thread of the task.
sent.lecture: The lecture usage (reading Leon) is checked by default: leon setup asks for it once for all the coding tools it sets up, with a box of the authorization page when leon setup opens it (to connect this computer, or again with --yes), otherwise in a terminal ([Y/n]: Enter accepts it); it never gives it by itself. A refusal is kept: it is not asked again until retirer-crochets. With it, at the start of each session or conversation, Leon places in the agent’s context the summary of your work threads on this repository (keys only: their id, branch, tools, dates, pull request numbers and states, number of linked sources) instead of your recent sessions, the lessons you accepted, and an instruction to read the thread of the task. For this, the start request also carries the usages of the tool and the Leon command of the computer, cited in the instruction. The agent can read your threads, their summaries and their state, and the memory of this repository that you can see, with leon threads, leon thread, leon search and leon versions, or with the MCP tools threads, thread and versions. The model provider of the tool sees what is placed and what is read. This usage never lets an agent write anything to Leon. The commands use the token of the computer: once one of your tools accepts it, they work for every agent on the computer; refusing it in a tool only removes, in that tool, what is placed at the start.
sent.resume: Session summaries (the resume usage) are optional: leon setup asks for them separately, once for all the coding tools it sets up, only in a terminal, never with --yes nor on the authorization page. A refusal is kept: leon setup does not ask again. To change your answer, run ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets (with --outil codex, --outil cursor or --outil antigravity for those tools; it removes the hooks and withdraws the consent of the tool), then leon setup again. Once a session with at least 6 of your messages has ended, the Leon server sends its actions, the state of its pull requests and the end of its exchanges (40,000 characters at most, secrets already masked) to Leon’s model provider, which writes the summary. Leon’s search finds it; it is never added to the context of a new session. Withdrawing your consent stops new summaries: retirer-crochets tells the Leon server this computer is connected to (only that server and account: one this computer used before is not told). If the computer is offline then, a summary already planned may still be written within an hour, and Leon later tells the server the computer is connected to by then: at the next session start of a tool that keeps its hooks, or when you run retirer-crochets again. The same usage also keeps the state of your work threads up to date: the actions, exchanges and summaries of these sessions, the state of their pull requests and the sources linked to the thread that you can see are sent to Leon’s model provider, which writes that state. Withdrawing your consent stops this too, once the Leon server is told.
sent.server: The hooks contact the server of the connection made by leon login, unless LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN are both set (a developer setup): those come first.

read.title: Reading Leon from a session
read.lead: Four commands read Leon’s memory of the repository they are run in and print it on standard output; they write nothing on disk. Your agent can run them, and so can you.
read.output: What they print starts with Leon’s guard line: it is data to check against the code and Git, never instructions. threads lists the threads of the repository (the work of your sessions, grouped by branch), the current branch first; thread prints one thread, with its state, sessions, pull requests and linked sources (without an id: the thread of the current branch); search searches Leon within this repository only; versions lists the readable versions of a thread’s state, or prints one with --read. Nothing restores a version from your computer.
read.consent: They need a connection and the reading usage (lecture, see “What is sent”), accepted by one of your code tools; leon setup offers it, checked by default. Without it, the server refuses, and the command says to run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal. The server notes each read (the tool and the source read).
read.external: Reading Leon does not count as bringing text from elsewhere into the session: neither these commands, nor the threads, thread, versions and remember tools of Leon’s MCP connector, when the MCP settings of your tool (Claude Code, Codex or Cursor) declare the leon server with the MCP address of the server you are connected to. Leon reads only that address there, never a header or a token. The connector’s search, fetch and briefing tools still count, as does any other MCP server.

updates.title: Updates
updates.auto: Leon’s command-line tool updates itself, at most once a day, when a session starts, from the server of your connection, and only over https. A local Leon (http://localhost) is updated by hand: ~/.leon/bin/leon update. An update touches neither your connection, nor your agreement, nor the launcher, nor the hooks.
updates.previous: To go back to the previous version, without network:
updates.previousNote: If the server still serves the same version, the next update, at the first session start after 24 hours, puts it back.

disconnect.title: Disconnect
disconnect.fromLeon: From Leon: {path}. This computer will stop sending your sessions.
disconnect.logout: From the computer: ~/.leon/bin/leon logout revokes the token of this computer and removes ~/.leon/connexion.json. If the server does not answer, the command says so and removes only the computer’s connection: revoke the computer in Settings then (see above).
disconnect.remove: ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets (French for “remove hooks”) removes Leon’s hooks from the Claude Code settings (your other settings stay as they are), withdraws your agreement (nothing is sent from Claude Code anymore), tells the Leon server this computer is connected to, and deletes the launcher once no other tool uses it and the server was told of each withdrawal. So run it before logout, which removes the connection it uses: once the launcher is gone, revoke the computer in Settings (see above).
disconnect.all: To leave completely: retirer-crochets (run it again until it no longer says the Leon server could not be told), then revoke the computer in Settings, then delete the ~/.leon folder.
disconnect.kept: Disconnecting does not delete what was already sent.

browser.title: The browser is on another computer
browser.text: For example over SSH or in a remote container: the return to 127.0.0.1 never arrives. Create a token in {path}, then, on the computer you want to connect:
browser.after: Paste the token when the command asks for it (it is not shown as you type), then finish with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup.

noTerminal.title: “No terminal is available”
noTerminal.text: The script put Node and the command-line tool in place, but it has no terminal to ask you its questions (this is the case from Claude Code or from a script). It prints the command that finishes the setup: run it in a terminal.

platform.title: Platform refused
platform.text: The script answers “not supported yet” (Windows, another architecture) or says your Linux uses musl (Alpine). It stops before writing anything. You need a Mac, or a Linux with glibc.

revoked.title: Computer revoked
revoked.text: If the computer was revoked in Settings, run the install command again, or ~/.leon/bin/leon setup: it sees the computer is no longer connected and starts the connection again.

interrupted.title: You created a workspace or reset your password along the way
interrupted.text: If you had to create a workspace or reset your password while authorizing, start the connection again with ~/.leon/bin/leon login, then finish with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup.

clone.title: From a Leon clone
clone.lead: For people who work on Leon. The launcher then runs your clone, with pnpm, instead of the installed copy; the hooks are the same.
clone.setup: The launcher (clone form), the connection and the hooks, like the single command.
clone.hooks: The launcher (clone form) and the Claude Code hooks only, after confirmation (--oui to skip it).
clone.note: Run them from the main clone, not from a temporary Git worktree: if it is deleted, the hooks stop working. In this form nothing updates itself: a clone is updated with git.

lecture.title: Reading Leon (usage "lecture", asked separately):
lecture.p1: At the start of each session or conversation, Leon places in the agent's context the summary of your work threads on this repository (keys only: their id, branch, tools, dates, pull request numbers and states, number of linked sources), which replaces the list of your recent sessions, the lessons you accepted, and an instruction to read the thread of its task. The model provider of the tool sees what it reads. This usage never lets an agent write anything to Leon.

claudeCode.copied: Instructions copied. Paste them into Claude Code.
claudeCode.withClaudeLead: Copy the instructions and paste them into Claude Code. It does the setup with you and tells you when to click “Authorize”. The boxes on that page are yours: it never ticks them or clicks for you.
claudeCode.instructions:
Install Leon on this computer and connect it to my coding tools.
1. Run this command in the terminal: {command}
If your sandbox blocks writing to ~/.leon or downloading from nodejs.org, ask me for permission to run it outside the sandbox.
2. If the script ends with “No terminal is available to ask you questions” and prints a last command that ends with “setup --url” followed by Leon's address: before you run it with the --yes option, copy to me, as is and without summarizing it, the text of what Leon will send (it is the “What is sent” section of {docs}) and wait for my explicit agreement. Never run --yes without my explicit agreement. If the script asks you questions instead of saying “No terminal is available…”, answer them with me.
3. Before you run that command, warn me that it opens my browser and waits for my click on “Authorize”, up to 5 minutes. Run it with a timeout of at least 5 minutes (your tool stops at 2 minutes by default) or in the background. The authorization page asks me to cancel if I did not run the command: remind me that you ran it for me. The page may also show boxes for usages (such as reading Leon), checked by default: they are mine. Never tick, untick or click anything on that page, and never open its address in a browser you control: only give it to me. If this computer is already connected, the command may open that page again for these boxes, and then waits about 100 seconds. If your sandbox stops it from opening the browser or listening on 127.0.0.1, ask me for permission to run it outside the sandbox. If the browser does not open, it prints the address to open: give it to me.
4. At the end, tell me which coding tools are connected and which Leon account this computer is connected to.
Never ask me for a token, read one or show one: the connection is made through the browser.
